claim: Each place specialises in tradables or non-tradables
category: c: needs increasing returns (the split itself is Ricardian)
evidence: In DFS the tradable/non-tradable split is endogenous (29.8% of goods non-traded) but every country makes both. In Model A without agglomeration cities are indifferent about what they make.

claim: A range of equilibria; history decides how many places are tradable
category: c: increasing returns with coordination failure (Graham 1923, Ethier 1982)
evidence: Model A: the set runs from 28.9% to 50.0% of cities; with no agglomeration it collapses to one point. DFS and the RV2023 engine (agglomeration up to 0.025) have one equilibrium.

claim: Places that lose tradables get non-tradable jobs, not new tradables, and stay that way
category: a for the shift to non-tradables; c for its persistence
evidence: In DFS an import shock also raises the non-traded share (29.8% to 43.1%) but through a 7.9% fall in the relative wage, and it reverses exactly. In Model A no lost tradable city is replaced while the economy stays in the set (shocks up to 21.1 points); without agglomeration all 5 of 5 are replaced. In the RV2023 engine a shocked sector returns in full when the shock is reversed.

claim: The loss hurts every non-tradable place and booms the remaining tradable ones; the rent share rises
category: b: dependent-economy price channel plus Rosen-Roback; c for persistence
evidence: Model A, X to 45%: wage in type-N cities -3.2%, their population -7.1%, their rents -13.7%, type-T wage +1.1%, rent share +0.01 points. The channel (a national price for non-tradables) is the Salter-Swan one.

claim: A boom in some tradables knocks out other tradable places (Dutch disease)
category: b: Dutch disease (Corden and Neary 1982); c for the lock-in
evidence: Model A with two tradable sectors: old-sector cities start dropping into non-tradables when the new sector's price is 9.0% higher; beyond about +12% the rest convert to the new sector instead. If both sectors boom no city switches.

claim: Too few tradable places lowers aggregate real income
category: c, and only if agglomeration runs out at the margin
evidence: With the papers' own linear agglomeration, real income is 1.45% HIGHER at the low edge of the set. It is 1.21% lower only when agglomeration is used up beyond the size at X.

claim: Fiscal contraction shrinks non-tradable places and booms tradable ones, in two regimes
category: b: real depreciation (Salter-Swan; DFS transfer problem); c for the two regimes
evidence: Model A, paper's financing: type-N cities start switching to tradables at G = -13.5; with a balanced budget none switch by G = -25. DFS: a transfer abroad lowers the relative wage 1.8%, with no regimes.

claim: Inside a country, absolute advantage rules; immobile factors are too small a cost share to restore competitiveness
category: a: Ricardo, "On Foreign Trade" (capital moves between provinces); the size claim is conditional
evidence: UK bottom-quartile areas pay 8.4% less for the same jobs; with property costs, unit costs are 5.1-9.4% lower. Cluster premiums: 4.7-20.2% (elasticity 0.02-0.04, size ratio 10-100). Model A's own gap at E is 23.3%.

claim: An advantage in tradables raises local nominal wages; one in non-tradables can lower them
category: b: Balassa-Samuelson inside a Rosen-Roback spatial equilibrium
evidence: RV2023 engine (R3): log wage on tradable advantage 0.47, on non-tradable advantage -0.11. Narrow benchmark (immobile labour): 0.55 and 0.04, so no sign reversal. Equal trade costs: 0.13 and 0.14.

claim: Places with tradable jobs are better off in real terms
category: false in both benchmarks; needs increasing returns or immobile people
evidence: Narrow benchmark: real income responds about equally to advantage in tradables (0.32) and non-tradables (0.29). Broad benchmark: utility barely moves with either (0.02, 0.01) because mobility equalises it.

claim: Measured (revenue) productivity can diverge from physical productivity
category: b: revenue versus physical productivity (Hsieh and Klenow 2009) in spatial equilibrium
evidence: Correlation of place wage (revenue productivity) with physical productivity: 0.87 in the narrow benchmark, 0.81 in R3, 0.11 in R3 without land.

claim: Sparsity bias accounts for about 75% of ITL3 earnings variation, two-thirds through the area effect
category: replicated, but it does not identify tradability
evidence: Rebuilt: adjusted R2 0.73, area differential 65.0% of the effect. But sector sparsity correlates only 0.34 with export shares, and export-share bias adds nothing beside sparsity (t = -0.8). Computing sparsity without London lowers R2 to 0.59.

claim: Places that lost sparsity bias in 1971-91 lost relative earnings
evidence: Needs the Census of Employment 1971-91 and New Earnings Survey county tables: not rebuilt in this round.

claim: Attracting non-tradable jobs crowds out tradables and locks places in
category: b: Dutch disease from public spending; c for the lock-in
evidence: Model A: raising public spending on non-tradables (paper's financing) starts pushing tradable cities into non-tradables at G = +11.0; by G = +25 the tradable share falls from 40% to 26.7%.

claim: The gains go to landowners in booming places
category: a/b: Ricardo's own theory of rent; Rosen-Roback
evidence: Model A import shock: rent share +0.01 percentage points; rents in type-N cities -13.7%. Workers' utility changes by +0.51%.
